extracted.intended_audience: researchers, graduate students, and practitioners in formal verification, interactive theorem proving, and automated reasoning (mathematicians, logicians, and computer scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: High-level survey and desiderata for verifying mathematics using formal methods: compares approaches (model checking vs ITP), discusses logical frameworks, assertion/proof languages, automation (decision/search procedures), and mathematical-knowledge management challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary use-cases for formal verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal methods can be used to verify correctness: (1) verifying that a circuit description, an algorithm, or a network or security protocol meets its specification; or (2) verifying that a mathematical statement is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two distinct application domains are highlighted (systems/engineering vs mathematics); approaches and tool choices should be driven by which use-case is targeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of verification approach: Model checking vs Interactive Theorem Proving
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches: Model checking: reduce to a finite state space, and test exhaustively. Interactive theorem proving: construct a formal axiomatic proof of correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use model checking when systems can be finitized for exhaustive analysis; use ITP when a formal axiomatic proof is required (e.g., deep mathematical claims or properties not amenable to state-space reduction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal proof objects should be extractable and independently verifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: In most systems, this proof object can be extracted and verified independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer systems and workflows that produce explicit proof artifacts (proof terms, scripts, certificates) that can be checked by small, trusted checkers to increase trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select an appropriate logical framework/foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different systems are based on different foundations: Mizar (Tarski–Grothendieck set theory); HOL/Isabelle/HOL light (simple type theory); Coq (constructive dependent type theory); ACL2 (primitive recursive arithmetic); PVS (classical dependent type theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The choice of foundation affects expressivity, style of proofs, and interoperability; pick the framework aligned with domain needs (e.g., constructive vs classical, dependent types vs simple types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof presentation/style: tactic-style vs declarative
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs can be written as tactic-style proof scripts (series of commands) or declarative proof scripts (structured, readable proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactic scripts can be concise and powerful; declarative scripts are often more readable and closer to mathematical prose. Consider maintainability, readability, and automation support when choosing style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and quality of mathematical libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Some systems have large mathematical libraries (elementary number theory, real/complex analysis, topology, measure-theoretic probability, abstract algebra, Galois theory, finite group theory, linear algebra, representation theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Library coverage strongly influences productivity; prefer systems with mature libraries in the target domain or invest in library development/translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect large-scale resource requirements for deep formalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Large formalizations (e.g., Feit–Thompson) involve substantial scale: ~150,000 lines of code, 4,000 definitions, 13,000 lemmas/theorems; original proofs may be hundreds of pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for substantial human and engineering effort for deep-theory formalizations; track metrics (LOC, defs, lemmas) and modularize work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration and verification of computation within proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational components (enumerating cases, proving nonlinear inequalities, showing infeasibility of linear programs) play an essential role (e.g., Flyspeck).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and use reliable mechanisms to incorporate and certify computations (certificates, verified code, checked outputs) rather than treating computation as untrusted black boxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational choices impact expressivity and identity principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Different axiomatic choices (e.g., univalent foundations) can change what can be expressed conveniently (e.g., adding an axiom that 'isomorphic structures are identical').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that adopting certain axioms or foundations (such as univalence) affects equality reasoning and can simplify or complicate formalizations; choose foundations to match the desired mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and readiness: steep learning curve and time costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive theorem proving is not 'ready for prime time.' There is a steep learning curve; verification can be time consuming and painful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh benefits against adoption costs; target use where formal verification gives high value (safety-critical systems, delicate proofs) or where investment in expertise is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-term practical targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Short term wins: verifying delicate, technical calculations by hand and verifying computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply formal methods first to tasks where they give immediate, high-value returns (technical calculations, computational checks) before attempting full formalizations of broad theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term infrastructure needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Long term: we need better libraries (and means to translate between them), automation (decision procedures, search procedures), ways to incorporate and verify computations, ways to express mathematical knowledge and expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in library development, interoperability/translation tools, automation research, and representation languages for mathematical expertise to scale formalization efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification at an appropriate level of abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not read, write, and understand mathematics at the level of a formal axiomatic system. Challenge: Develop ways of verifying mathematics at an appropriate level of abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assertion and proof languages and tool support that reflect the abstraction and informal practices of mathematicians (higher-level constructs, notation, and modularity) rather than forcing low-level formal detail everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertion language must model implicit mathematical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A lot of implicit knowledge goes into reading and understanding ordinary mathematical statements (e.g., summation indices, embedding of N in R, what 'G' denotes, meaning of multiplication 'ab', that 'p' is a prime etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertion languages should encode and make explicit common implicit assumptions (type/role annotations, ambient structures, coercions) to avoid verbose low-level encodings and to match mathematicians' expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertion language must support algebraic and structural hierarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: The hierarchy of algebraic structures involves subclasses, reducts, instances, embeddings, and uniform constructions (e.g., every abelian group is a group; additive part of a ring is an abelian group; integers embed in reals; automorphisms of a field form a group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide mechanisms for inheritance, coercions, and generic constructions so notation and theorems can be reused across related structures; support for overloading and canonical embeddings is useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate reuse of notation, definitions, and facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages: Reusing notation (0, +, a·b), reusing definitions (sums), reusing facts (identities involving sums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design libraries and languages to maximize reuse (generic definitions, well-chosen abstractions) to prevent duplication and ease formal development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof language must capture proof structure and workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs work in subtle ways: setting out structure, introducing local hypotheses and subgoals, unpacking definitions, invoking background facts, carrying out calculations, and so on. Challenge: Develop formal models of everyday mathematical proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof languages and interfaces should support hierarchical structure, local context management, readable presentation of subgoals, and facilities for invoking background facts and calculations in natural ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish domain-general vs domain-specific automated methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated techniques fall into domain-general methods (propositional, first-order, higher-order theorem proving, equality reasoning, Nelson–Oppen) and domain-specific methods (linear arithmetic, nonlinear real arithmetic, algebraic methods such as Gröbner bases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose or combine methods according to problem structure: domain-specific procedures excel on homogeneous mathematical domains; domain-general methods provide broader coverage but may need heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate search procedures from decision procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated techniques include search procedures and decision procedures; decision procedures solve theory-specific logical validity, search procedures explore proof/search spaces heuristically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use decision procedures where decidability and certificates are available; use search procedures (resolution, tableaux, model-based) for broader or heuristic reasoning, and integrate them when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer restricted fragments (e.g., universal) for practicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes it is better to focus on the universal fragment: some theories are only decidable at this level; it can be more efficient; one can use certificates; a lot of mathematical reasoning is close to quantifier-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target decidable or efficiently solvable fragments of theories where they capture the bulk of problems encountered in practice, and provide certificate mechanisms for trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits: practical feasibility over theoretical decidability
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision procedures are often infeasible; undecidability sets in quickly; decidability results do not bear directly on practical problems (a decision procedure that runs too slowly on your examples is worthless).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on empirical performance and relevance to real examples; theoretical decidability is insufficient—measure and optimize actual runtime and behavior on target benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage and understand strengths/limitations of search procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Search procedures (resolution, paramodulation, tableaux, model-based) have different strengths: some do well on wide-and-shallow problems, others on narrow-and-deep; they often do poorly on domain-specific reasoning like arithmetic and may fail on straightforward inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select search engines that match problem shape and combine them with domain-specific solvers; provide heuristics and guidance (e.g., Sledgehammer) to bridge gaps between general search and library/theory knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine decision procedures under sound conditions (Nelson–Oppen/SMT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nelson–Oppen theorem: if T1 and T2 are stably infinite and their universal fragments are decidable, and languages are disjoint except equality, then the universal fragment of T1 ∪ T2 is decidable. SMT architecture: SAT solver proposes assignments; theory solvers report conflicts; the SAT solver uses that info.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design combination frameworks respecting required conditions (disjoint signatures, stable infiniteness where needed) and adopt SMT-style architectures to integrate propositional search with specialized theory solvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outstanding combination challenges: quantifiers, non-disjoint signatures, and hybridization
rubrics_metrics.description: We are still trying to understand how to handle quantifiers in such a framework, to combine theories with non-disjoint signatures, and to combine general search procedures with domain-specific methods and computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and engineering are needed to devise instantiation strategies, bridging translations, and hybrid search/decision integrations that handle real-world heterogeneous problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build on core logical/theoretical foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary successes build on core results in logic: formal axiomatic systems, semantics and completeness proofs, cut elimination, normalization and the lambda calculus, Skolemization, decision procedures, model theory, Craig interpolation. The theory guides the enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain strong theoretical grounding in system design, combining theoretical insights (e.g., normalization, interpolation) with practical engineering to ensure soundness and guide heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Knowledge Management (MKM): interoperability problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems in importing results between provers: different foundational frameworks, different axiomatic bases, different definitions (reals as Cauchy sequences vs Dedekind cuts), different side conditions (x/0), proof terms get really big.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address interoperability by standardizing representations where feasible, developing translation/transport mechanisms, and designing compact proof representations or certificates for cross-system exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: MKM needs: search, relevance assessment, and communication between tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Other MKM questions: How can we search for mathematical theorems in a large library? How can we assess relevance? How can questions and partial results be communicated between different reasoning tools?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop indexing, semantic search, relevance metrics, and protocols/APIs for exchanging partial proofs and queries between systems to enable tool cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary benefits/goals of formal methods for mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal methods are valuable to mathematics: they provide additional precision; they provide strong guarantees of correctness; they make it possible to verify mathematical computation; they make it possible to use automation in a reliable way; they assist in the storing, finding, and communicating mathematical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal methods to achieve these concrete benefits; design projects and tools to deliver precision, trustable guarantees, verifiable computations, reliable automation, and MKM support.
